title: HTTP Requests and Responses
about: What your browser asks a website for, and what comes back.

cards.prompt:
Your [[browser]] has to **ask** for every file a page needs, one request per file.

A page has its text (one file) and 3 photos, none saved yet. How many requests?
cards.explanation: One for the text plus one per photo: 1 + 3 = **4**. The browser gets the text first, and only then learns it needs the photos.
cards.hint: Count every file, including the text itself.
cards.nudge: The photos aren't the only files: the page's text is a file too.

cards.title: Ask and answer
cards.body:
That asking follows a [[protocol]] called **HTTP**. Your [[browser]] sends a **request**, like `GET /news`: a **method** (what to do) and a **path** (which page).

The [[server]] replies with a **response**: a **status code** (how it went), then the **body**, the content itself. Web pages are written in **HTML**.

cards.prompt: Match each part of an [[HTTP]] conversation to its job.

pairs.right: What you want the server to do
Which page or file you want
The content itself, like the page's HTML

cards.explanation: The **method** (the action) and the **path** (which item) go out in the request. The **status code** and the **body** come back: first how it went, then the content.
cards.hint: Like ordering at a café: what to do, which item, whether they could, and what you get handed.
cards.nudge: Two go out in the request and two come back; the status code is the short "how did it go" part.

cards.prompt:
**GET** means "please give me this"; **POST** means "please take this data".

Which does your [[browser]] use for each?
cards.explanation: Watching, viewing and opening all **fetch**, so they're **GET**. Commenting, logging in and uploading **send your data**, so they're **POST**.
cards.hint: Is data coming **to** you, or are you sending something of yours **to** the server?
cards.nudge: Logging in feels like "getting in", but your password travels to the server: which method sends data?

cards.prompt: A **status code**'s first digit says how it went: **2** fine, **4** a problem with the request, **5** a problem on the server.
cards.explanation: **2** worked. **4** means the request was the problem (404: nothing there), and **5** means the server failed (500: an error inside it; 503: busy or down).
cards.hint: Ignore the words for a moment and read only the first digit of each code.
cards.nudge: Some words sound alarming, but only the first digit decides.

cards.prompt: `curl -I` (capital **I**) shows the status code and labelled lines (**headers**). A **3** code means "moved"; `Location` gives the new address. Run `curl -I http://example.com/old-news`.
cards.intro: Simulated Linux terminal. Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: Get the response headers for the home page
commands.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Content-Length: 1256
Date: Tue, 29 Sep 2026 10:20:15 GMT
Server: nginx

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: http://example.com/news
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 169
Date: Tue, 29 Sep 2026 10:20:21 GMT
Server: nginx

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: text/html
Content-Length: 153
Date: Tue, 29 Sep 2026 10:20:27 GMT
Server: nginx

cards.explanation: `/old-news` gave **301 Moved Permanently**, and its `Location` line says `http://example.com/news`. A [[browser]] follows that by itself.
cards.hint: Run it on `/old-news`, then find the line starting with `Location`.
cards.nudge: The first line only says it moved: the new address is on its own line further down.

cards.prompt: A page shows **500 Internal Server Error**. What does that say about your own connection?

options.text: It works: a reply came, so the server's at fault
It's broken: your Wi-Fi dropped out mid-request
options.nudge: With no Wi-Fi, no response would arrive at all: what does a status code prove?

options.text: It works, but you typed the address wrong
options.nudge: A wrong address is a problem with the request: which first digit did that have?

options.text: Nothing: a 500 could mean working or broken
options.nudge: Could any status code reach you over a broken connection?

cards.explanation: A **5** means the **server** had a problem, and any response arriving proves your connection worked. A typo would give a **4** code, like 404.
cards.hint: Two clues: the first digit of the code, and the fact that a response arrived at all.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **HTTP**: the [[browser]] requests, the [[server]] responds.
- **GET** fetches things; **POST** sends your data to the server.
- Status codes: **2** fine, **3** moved, **4** request problem, **5** server problem.

Next: keeping all of this private with [[HTTPS]].
